title: A Prayer of the Afflicted
sum: A person worn down by sickness and grief pours out his complaint: his days vanish like smoke, his bones burn, he is like a lone bird among ruins, his enemies use his name as a curse, and he feels that God has picked him up and thrown him aside (102:1–11). Then the psalm turns from the sufferer to Zion. God sits enthroned forever, and the time has come to pity the city whose very stones and dust his servants love. When he rebuilds Zion, the nations will fear his name, and a people not yet born will praise him (102:12–22).

The last section returns to the sufferer, whose strength has failed halfway through life (102:23–24). He sets his short days against God's endless years: the earth and heavens God made will wear out like clothing, "But you are he, / and your years will never run out" (102:27). Hebrews 1:10–12 quotes 102:25–27 from the Greek as words addressed to the Son. The church counts Psalm 102 among the seven penitential psalms. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 101, and in Hebrew Bibles each verse number is one higher than here, because the title is verse 1.
readings: Read as one sufferer's prayer
The title invites any afflicted person to pray it. The images of fever, fasting, sleeplessness and mockery are those of a personal lament, and the end is a plea not to die young.
Read as Zion's lament

Many scholars hear the voice of ruined Jerusalem, or of an exile who speaks for it: the rubble, the dust, the prisoners and "the children of death" (102:14, 20) fit the years after 587 or 586 BC, and the hope is the city's rebuilding.
Read through Hebrews

Christians, following Hebrews 1:10–12, read the closing verses as the Father's words to the Son, the Creator who outlasts creation; some Fathers read the whole psalm as the prayer of Christ in his suffering.

views.H: The title names no author, only a situation: "a person in misery." Readers who take titles as history treat it as an instruction for use, not a claim about who wrote it. Jewish and Christian tradition has often heard an exile in Babylon praying for Zion.
views.C: Critical scholars usually date the psalm to the exile or soon after, when Zion lay in ruins but hope of rebuilding was alive (compare Isaiah 40–55 and Lamentations). Many think a personal lament (102:1–11, 23–24) was combined with a hymn of hope for Zion (102:12–22, 25–28), or that the sufferer is a figure for the city. 11QPs-a from Qumran preserves parts of the psalm, as reported by The Dead Sea Scrolls Bible. Witnesses checked for this part, Psalms 102–106: the Hebrew through the site's literal text and Leningrad Codex readings; the Greek in Tischendorf's printed Vaticanus (with its apparatus for Alexandrinus, Sinaiticus and others) and in Rahlfs' critical text; the site's Plain of 1 Chronicles 16, Genesis, Exodus and Numbers. The Dead Sea Scrolls, the Syriac, the Targum and Jerome's Latin from the Hebrew are given as reported by the sources named.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 101. Psalm 102 is the fifth of the seven penitential psalms of the Western church, prayed in Lent and on Ash Wednesday. In the Orthodox Psalter it opens the fourteenth kathisma (Greek Psalms 101–104).
views.J: Jewish prayer books include Psalm 102 among the psalms said in times of trouble and illness. Medieval commentators such as Rashi and Radak read it as the prayer of the exiles, with "the time to be kind to her" (102:13) as the end of exile. 102:18, "a people that will be created," was read as the generation of redemption.
views.X: Hebrews 1:10–12 makes 102:25–27 an address to the Son, part of its argument that the Son is greater than the angels. Augustine read the psalm as the voice of the whole Christ, head and body, and the lone bird on the roof as Christ alone in his passion. Many Christian readers draw from 102:26–27 the hope of a new creation (2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 21:1).

deep.b:
Hebrews 1:5–13 quotes seven passages to show that the Son is above the angels. The sixth is Psalm 102:25–27, introduced as what God says "to the Son" (Hebrews 1:8; Hebrews 1:10). In a fresh rendering of the Greek of Hebrews 1:10–12: "You, Lord, at the beginning laid the earth's foundation, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They will be lost, but you stay on; all of them will grow old like clothing. Like a wrap you will roll them up, like clothing, and they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will not run out."

Two features certainly come from the Greek Psalter, not the Hebrew: the word "Lord" (see the variant at 102:25) and "you are the same" for the Hebrew "you are he" (102:27). A third is disputed: "roll them up" is the reading of Codex Vaticanus and a few other Greek copies, while the main Greek text has "change them," as the Hebrew does (see the variant at 102:26); those copies may have been brought into line with Hebrews. The address "Lord" makes it easier to hear the verse as spoken to someone. Some scholars also point to the Greek of 102:23–24, where God "answered him" and the speaker is told about the shortness of days, as a dialogue that early Christians could read as the Father speaking to the Son. In the Hebrew, the psalmist speaks to God throughout.

For Hebrews, the Son is the one through whom God made the worlds (Hebrews 1:2), so creation words addressed to the LORD apply to him. Commentators such as Attridge, Lane and Koester discuss how far the author relied on the Greek wording. Hebrews 13:8, "Jesus Christ, yesterday and today the same, and to the ages" (a fresh rendering), echoes the "you are the same" of this psalm.

The psalm is built on a contrast of time. The sufferer's "days" run out in smoke (102:3), are like a lengthening evening shadow (102:11), and are cut short in the middle (102:23–24). God's "years" go on "through generation after generation" (102:24) and "will never run out" (102:27). Between them stands Zion, whose "hour" has come (102:13). The sufferer finds hope not in his own recovery, which the psalm never reports, but in God's permanence and in the future of "your servants' children" (102:28). The same move appears in Psalm 90, which opens Book IV: "from the ages past to the ages to come, you are God" (Psalm 90:2) set against human life that withers like grass.

echoes: Psalm 90:2–6; Psalm 6:2–7; Lamentations 1:13; Lamentations 4:8; Isaiah 51:6; Isaiah 40:6–8; Isaiah 34:4; Hebrews 1:10–12; Hebrews 13:8; 2 Peter 3:10–13; Revelation 21:1

settings.what: A lament of a dying sufferer that becomes a prayer for Zion
settings.by: An unnamed "person in misery" (the title); the psalm names no author
settings.to: The LORD; the hope for Zion (102:12–22) is spoken to God but meant to be heard by the community and "the next generation" (102:18)
settings.when: Most scholars place it in the exile or the early return, between about 587 and 450 BC, when Zion's stones lay in ruins (102:14)
settings.why: To give the afflicted words to bring their misery to God, and to set their short life against God's endless years and his promise to rebuild Zion
settings.readers: For Jews in Babylon or in a ruined Judah, the psalm joined private sickness and national ruin: the same God who would rebuild Zion was the one to whom a dying person could cry.
views: Some read it as the prayer of a sick individual who also hopes for Zion (Goldingay).
Others read the sufferer as a figure for Zion or for the exiled people (Hossfeld and Zenger; Allen discusses both).

traditions.q: Is the LORD of Psalm 102:25–27, the maker of earth and heaven, the Son himself?
views: Yes: the Son is true God, of one essence with the Father, through whom all things were made, as the Creed says; Hebrews rightly applies the Creator's words to him.
Yes: creation is the common work of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and the Son is God from God; Hebrews 1 shows the Son as Creator (Catechism 291).

Yes: the Son is the eternal God, of one substance with the Father (Westminster Confession 8.2); Calvin argued that Hebrews applies the psalm to Christ because the God who rebuilds Zion is revealed in him.
No: Jehovah is the Creator, and the Son is his first creation, through whom he made other things; Hebrews applies the words to the Son as God's agent in creation, not as Jehovah himself.
Yes, in their own sense: Jesus Christ was "the Great Jehovah of the Old Testament" and, under the direction of his Father, the Creator of the earth; he is a separate being from the Father.

title: Bless the LORD, My Soul
sum: The singer calls on his own soul to bless the LORD and not forget his gifts: he forgives, heals, ransoms from the Pit, crowns with loyal love and renews youth like the eagle's (103:1–5). He moves from himself to Israel: God showed Moses his ways, and the psalm repeats God's own words to Moses at Sinai, "Compassionate and gracious is the LORD, / slow to anger and great in loyal love" (103:8; Exodus 34:6). God does not treat us as our sins deserve; he removes them as far as sunrise is from sunset and feels for those who fear him as a father for his children (103:9–13).

Human life is short as grass, because "he keeps in mind that we are dust" (103:14–16), but God's loyal love lasts from age to age for those who keep his covenant (103:17–18). The psalm ends by calling the angels, the heavenly armies and all creation to bless the LORD, and finally the singer's own soul again (103:19–22). Psalm 104 begins and ends with the same call. In Greek and Latin Bibles this psalm is Psalm 102.
readings: Read as thanksgiving
The opening list of benefits sounds like the thanks of someone forgiven and healed, perhaps after an illness like the one in Psalm 102.
Read as a hymn of the covenant
Its center is Exodus 34:6–7, God's self-description after the golden calf. The psalm is a meditation on that creed and on mercy outlasting sin.
Read as the soul's sermon to itself
The singer speaks to his own nefesh (103:1, 2, 22). It has often been read as a model for private devotion, a person reminding himself of what God has done.

views.H: The title says "Of David." Readers who take the title as history hear David, forgiven after his sin with Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12:13) or after the census (2 Samuel 24:10–25), and some connect the "healing" to that forgiveness.
views.C: Critical scholars mostly date the psalm after the exile, because of its language (several late Hebrew forms, including Aramaic-style suffixes in 103:3–5) and its closeness to the theology of Isaiah 40–66 and Jonah 4:2. It belongs with Psalm 104 as a pair framed by "Bless the LORD, my soul." Parts of the psalm are preserved in Dead Sea copies, including 2QPs, as reported by The Dead Sea Scrolls Bible.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 102. In the Orthodox Divine Liturgy it is the first antiphon (the typika) on many days, and it is one of the six psalms of the Hexapsalmos at Matins. Western churches use it at funerals and in the Liturgy of the Hours. Henry Francis Lyte's hymn "Praise, my soul, the King of heaven" (1834) paraphrases it.
views.J: The Talmud (Berakhot 10a) says that the five times "Bless the LORD, my soul" appear in Psalms 103 and 104 correspond to five ways the soul resembles God: it fills the body, sees but is not seen, sustains the body, is pure, and dwells in the innermost rooms. 103:8 echoes the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, which Jews recite on fasts and holy days, and 103:13 is used in the penitential Selichot prayers.
views.X: Christians have read the psalm as the gospel in the Old Testament: forgiveness, healing and redemption from death. 103:3 is cited in debates about healing (see below). 103:13 is often compared with Jesus' teaching on God as Father (Luke 15:20; Luke 11:13), and 103:20–21 is used in teaching about angels.

deep.h: The creed of Exodus 34 in Psalm 103
deep.b: After the golden calf, Moses asks, "let me know your ways" (Exodus 33:13), and God passes by calling out, "The LORD, the LORD, a God compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). Psalm 103 recalls both moments: "He let Moses know his ways" (103:7) and "Compassionate and gracious is the LORD, / slow to anger and great in loyal love" (103:8). It then leaves out the second half of the creed, that God "will by no means leave guilt unpunished" and brings the fathers' guilt home to the third and fourth generation (Exodus 34:7), and replaces it with its own lines: he will not accuse forever (103:9), he does not repay us as our sins deserve (103:10), and his loyal love reaches "the children of their children" (103:17), where Exodus has guilt reaching "the children and the children's children." Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2, Nehemiah 9:17 and Psalm 145:8 also quote the creed, each in its own way.
deep.refs: 103:7–10; 103:17; Exodus 33:13; Exodus 34:6–7; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Nehemiah 9:17; Psalm 86:15

deep.b: 103:3–5 lists five things God does, each a participle in Hebrew: he pardons, heals, ransoms, crowns, fills. Sin comes first, then sickness, then death ("the Pit"), and the list ends with renewed life. Ancient Israel often linked sickness with sin (Psalm 32:3–5; Psalm 38:3), so forgiveness and healing come together, as they do in Jesus' healing of the paralyzed man (Mark 2:5–12). The Aramaic-style suffixes on these words ("your" as -ekhi) are one of the signs scholars use to date the psalm late.

echoes: Exodus 33:13; Exodus 34:6–7; Numbers 14:18; Isaiah 40:6–8; Isaiah 40:31; Isaiah 55:8–9; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Psalm 104:1; Psalm 145:8; Luke 1:50; Luke 15:20; Mark 2:5–12; 1 Peter 1:24–25

settings.what: A hymn of thanks for forgiveness, built on God's words to Moses
settings.by: David, according to the title; a singer speaking to his own soul
settings.to: Himself first ("my soul"), then the congregation ("us," 103:10–14), and finally the angels and all creation (103:20–22)
settings.when: Tradition places it in David's reign; most scholars date it after the exile, about 500–300 BC, on the basis of its language
settings.why: To keep the people from forgetting what God had done, and to answer the fear that sin had used up God's patience: his loyal love outlasts both sin and death
settings.readers: After the exile, when Israel knew that its sins had led to disaster, the psalm assured the community that God "has not done to us what our sins have earned" (103:10) and that his covenant still stood.
views: Traditional readers hear David's own thanks for forgiveness.
Most critical scholars read it as a post-exilic hymn shaped by Exodus 34 and the prophets (Allen; Hossfeld and Zenger).

traditions.q: Does "he heals every sickness you have" (103:3) promise physical healing to believers now?
views: Yes: divine healing is part of the gospel, and deliverance from sickness is provided for in Christ's atonement; believers may pray for it with faith (Fundamental Truths 12).

God can heal, and the Church prays for the sick and anoints them; but the sacrament does not promise bodily cure in every case, and suffering joined to Christ's can itself be healing (Catechism 1500–1513).

Holy unction is offered for healing of soul and body, and miracles of healing are expected through prayer and the saints; healing is a gift, not a guarantee, and bodily death awaits all until the resurrection.

God heals as he wills, often through means such as medicine; the psalm's chief benefit is forgiveness, and full healing belongs to the resurrection. Calvin read 103:3 as including bodily recovery, granted for the soul's good.

title: The World God Made
sum: The psalm begins where Psalm 103 ended, "Bless the LORD, my soul," and turns at once to the world. God is clothed in light and stretches out the sky like a tent; he builds his upper rooms in the waters, rides the clouds and makes winds and fire his servants (104:1–4). He set the earth firm and drove back the waters that covered it, giving them a boundary they may not cross (104:5–9). Then he turned the waters into springs and rain that feed wild donkeys and birds, grass for cattle, and bread, wine and oil for people; the cedars, storks, ibex and rock badgers all have their place (104:10–18).

The moon marks the seasons and the sun its setting; the lions hunt at night, and people work by day (104:19–23). "LORD, how many things you have made!" (104:24). The sea teems with creatures, ships, and Leviathan, made to play in it (104:25–26). All living things wait for God to feed them; when he takes back their breath they die, and when he sends it out they are created (104:27–30). The singer prays that God may rejoice in his works, vows to praise him all his life, and asks that sinners vanish from the earth (104:31–35). In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 103.
readings: Read beside Genesis 1
The psalm moves loosely through the same order as the creation days, from light to people and from the sky to the sea, but it tells creation as a living, present activity.
Read beside the Hymn to the Aten
Many scholars see in 104:20–30 the influence of the Egyptian Great Hymn to the Aten, perhaps through later Egyptian or Canaanite hymns.
Read as a nature psalm
Readers have taken it as the Bible's great poem of ecology: every creature has its place, food and time, and God delights in all of it.

views.H: The Hebrew psalm has no title; the Greek adds "Of David." Readers who take titles as history therefore follow the Greek and hear David, the shepherd and singer, or treat it as an anonymous temple hymn. The Talmud joins Psalms 103 and 104 as songs of David (Berakhot 10a).
views.C: Critical scholars date the psalm anywhere from the monarchy to after the exile. Its imagery draws on the storm-god pictures of Canaan (Baal riding the clouds; the battle with the sea) and its middle section on Egyptian sun hymns. Several copies were found at Qumran (4QPs-d, 4QPs-e, 4QPs-l, 2QPs and 11QPs-a), some in a different order, as reported in published editions not checked for this page.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 103. It is the opening psalm of Orthodox Vespers every evening (the Proemiac Psalm), sung as the lamps are lit. The Catholic Church uses 104:30, "Send forth your Spirit," as the responsorial psalm at Pentecost. Robert Grant's hymn "O worship the King" (1833) paraphrases it.
views.J: Jews recite Psalm 104 on the New Moon (Rosh Chodesh), because 104:19 speaks of the moon and the appointed times, and in many Ashkenazi communities after the Sabbath afternoon service in winter. The Talmud (Berakhot 10a) reads 104:35 through Beruriah: pray that sins, not sinners, come to an end.
views.X: Christians have read 104:30 of the Holy Spirit as the giver of life, as in the Nicene Creed. Hebrews 1:7 quotes 104:4 from the Greek about angels. The psalm was a key text for medieval and modern theologies of creation, from Basil's homilies on the six days to modern Christian environmental ethics.

deep.b:
The psalm touches each of the six days, in roughly the same order, but tells them as God's ongoing care, not as a finished week:

Genesis 1Psalm 104
Day 1: light (Genesis 1:3)God wraps himself in light (104:2)
Day 2: the dome divides the waters (Genesis 1:6)The heavens spread like a tent; God's upper rooms in the waters (104:2–3)
Day 3: waters gathered, dry ground, plants (Genesis 1:9; Genesis 1:11)The waters flee to their place; springs, grass, crops and trees (104:5–18)
Day 4: lights for "the appointed times" (Genesis 1:14)The moon "to keep the appointed times," the sun (104:19–23)
Day 5: sea creatures and great sea monsters (Genesis 1:20–21)The sea full of creatures, and Leviathan (104:25–26)
Day 6: animals and people, and food given (Genesis 1:24–29)All creatures wait for God to give them food (104:27–28)
Day 7: God rests and sees all is "very good" (Genesis 1:31; Genesis 2:2)"Let the LORD be glad in what he has made" (104:31)

The differences matter as much. Genesis 1 has no struggle with the waters; the psalm has God's "scolding" and "thunder" driving them back (104:7), like the older poetic tradition of God's battle with the sea. Genesis makes the sea monsters creatures; the psalm makes Leviathan a pet. Genesis gives people plants to eat; the psalm adds wine and oil. And where Genesis ends with God's rest, the psalm ends with death and renewal: creatures die when God gathers back their breath and are created when he sends it out (104:29–30), a picture of creation that goes on every day. Whether the psalm knew Genesis 1 in its present form, or both drew on a shared tradition, is debated.

deep.h: Psalm 104 and the Hymn to the Aten
deep.b:
The Great Hymn to the Aten was carved in the tomb of Ay at Amarna in Egypt in the time of the pharaoh Akhenaten (about 1350–1334 BC), who worshiped the sun disk, the Aten, as the one god. Since James Breasted in the early 1900s, scholars have noticed close parallels with Psalm 104:20–30. In paraphrase, the hymn says that when the sun sets the land lies in darkness as if dead, lions come out of their dens and snakes bite (compare 104:20–21); when the sun rises, people wake, wash and go to work (104:22–23); ships sail up and down the river, and the fish leap toward the light (104:25–26); every creature lives when the sun rises and dies when it sets (104:27–30); and the hymn exclaims at how many are the god's works (104:24).

The order of the scenes is close, and some scholars, such as John Day, think the psalmist knew a form of the hymn, perhaps passed through later Egyptian sun hymns or Phoenician adaptations. Others think both draw on common Near Eastern ways of praising a creator. The differences are just as striking. In the psalm the sun is a creature that "knows where it sets" (104:19), not a god; night and the lions belong to God's good order, not to the god's absence; and the God of the psalm is worshiped not through a king, as the Aten was through Akhenaten alone, but by anyone who sings. There is no evidence of a direct line from Akhenaten to Moses, an idea that Freud and others proposed.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the psalm's turn to sinners
deep.b: Many readers find the sudden wish of 104:35, that sinners be finished off from the earth, out of place in a psalm of joy in creation. My own reading is that it is not out of place. The whole psalm has been about God giving each creature its place and setting boundaries: the waters "will not pass over" the line he drew (104:9), the lions keep to the night, people keep to the day. The sinner is the one creature that refuses its place. The prayer that sinners be "finished off" (yittammu) uses the same root as "complete" and asks that the world be made whole by removing what spoils it, as the flood narrative imagines and as Revelation 21:1 imagines without the sea. This is an observation about the psalm's structure, not a view I have found argued in this form by a commentator, though Beruriah's reading (sins, not sinners) points the same way.

echoes: Genesis 1:1–2:3; Genesis 8:22; Job 38:4–41; Psalm 8:3–8; Psalm 29:3–10; Psalm 103:1; Psalm 145:15–16; Proverbs 8:22–31; Isaiah 40:12–26; Matthew 6:26–30; Hebrews 1:7; Acts 14:17

settings.what: A hymn to God as creator and sustainer of the world
settings.by: An unnamed singer; the Greek title says "Of David"
settings.to: God, mostly in the second person, with lines about him in the third person; the singer's own soul (104:1, 35)
settings.when: Uncertain: scholars range from the monarchy (because of the Canaanite and Egyptian parallels) to after the exile (because of the pairing with Psalm 103 and the closeness to Genesis 1)
settings.why: To praise God for a world in which every creature has its place, food and time, and to confess that all life depends on his breath from moment to moment
settings.readers: For Israel among empires that worshiped the sun, the sea and the storm, the psalm put all of them in their place as creatures of the one God, and it gave ordinary farmers and sailors a way to see their daily work and food as his gift.
views: Some scholars think the psalm adapts an Egyptian sun hymn (Day; Breasted).
Others think the parallels come from common ways of praising a creator across the Near East (Hoffmeier; Kraus).

title: He Keeps His Covenant in Mind
sum: A call to give thanks, sing and remember opens the psalm, addressed to "you seed of Abraham" (105:1–6). Its theme is that God "keeps his covenant in mind for all time," the promise of Canaan he made to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (105:7–11). When the ancestors were few, wandering among nations, God protected them and warned kings, "Hands off my anointed ones!" (105:12–15). These first fifteen verses are also part of the song David's singers sing in 1 Chronicles 16:8–22.

The psalm then retells the story. God called a famine, but had sent Joseph ahead; Joseph was sold, chained, tested and freed, and became ruler of Pharaoh's house (105:16–22). Israel went to Egypt and grew strong, until God turned the Egyptians against them (105:23–25). He sent Moses and Aaron and struck Egypt with signs: darkness, blood, frogs, the swarm and gnats, hail, locusts, and the death of the firstborn (105:26–36). He led Israel out with silver and gold, sheltered them with cloud and fire, fed them with quail and bread from heaven, gave them water from the rock, and brought them into the land, "so that they would keep his rules" (105:37–45). In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 104, and the Greek gives it the title "Alleluia."
readings: Read as covenant history
The psalm tells history as the outworking of one promise. Everything from the famine to the conquest happens because "he kept in mind his holy word / and Abraham his servant" (105:42).
Read with Psalm 106
Psalm 105 tells the story as God's faithfulness, with Israel's sins left out; Psalm 106 tells the same story as Israel's unfaithfulness. The two belong together.
Read in 1 Chronicles 16
Chronicles uses the first part of the psalm at the ark's arrival in Jerusalem, turning a history of the patriarchs into a call to David's people to remember the covenant.

views.H: The Hebrew psalm has no title. Readers who take titles as history look to 1 Chronicles 16:7, which places 105:1–15 in David's day, when "David first gave the task of thanking the LORD to Asaph and his kinsmen." On that reading David composed or commissioned the song.
views.C: Most critical scholars date the psalm after the exile, because of its interest in the land promised to a small people living among nations and its close use of the Torah's narratives (Genesis, Exodus and Numbers, perhaps in their finished form). Most think Chronicles drew on the psalm rather than the reverse. 11QPs-a and 4QPs-e from Qumran preserve parts of it, sometimes with small differences (see the variants); as reported by The Dead Sea Scrolls Bible.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 104. The Hodu prayer (1 Chronicles 16:8–36), which contains 105:1–15, is said every morning in the Jewish service (Pesukei deZimra). Christian lectionaries read parts of the psalm with the Joseph and exodus stories, and Coverdale's Prayer Book line "the iron entered into his soul" passed into English speech (see the note on Joseph's fetters).
views.J: Jewish readers have treated the psalm as a summary of God's providence over Israel, especially the Joseph story (105:16–22) as proof that God works through human evil (Genesis 50:20). Medieval commentators discussed why the plague order differs from Exodus. The Hodu prayer keeps 105:1–15 in the daily liturgy.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in Joseph, sold, chained and raised up to rule, a type of Christ, and in the manna and the rock, types of Christ as bread and water of life (John 6:31–35; 1 Corinthians 10:1–4). 105:15, "Hands off my anointed ones," has been used in many churches to discourage criticism of leaders, a use the context does not support (see the note).

deep.b:
105:1–15 appears again in 1 Chronicles 16:8–22. The site's Plain of 1 Chronicles 16 is used here wherever the Hebrew is the same. The Hebrew differs in these places:

VersePsalm 1051 Chronicles 16
105:6 / 1 Chronicles 16:13"you seed of Abraham, his servant""you seed of Israel, his servant"
105:8 / 1 Chronicles 16:15"He keeps his covenant in mind" (zakhar)"Keep his covenant in mind" (zikhru)
105:12 / 1 Chronicles 16:19"When they were men who could be counted""when you were" few (bihyotkhem)
105:14 / 1 Chronicles 16:21"anyone" (adam)"any man" (le'ish)

There are also small differences of spelling (Isaac is spelled with a different letter in 105:9), of particles (Chronicles adds "and" in 1 Chronicles 16:20 and lacks the object marker in 1 Chronicles 16:11), and a preposition in 105:15. The pattern is consistent: Chronicles speaks directly to its audience ("Keep ... in mind," "you were") and names Israel rather than Abraham, so that the song addresses the people standing before the ark. After 105:15, Chronicles continues with Psalm 96 and then with 106:1 and 106:47–48. Since the Plain here keeps the psalm's own Hebrew in these places, the English differs from 1 Chronicles 16 in 105:6, 105:8, 105:12 and 105:14; in 105:15 only a Hebrew preposition differs, and the English is the same.

deep.h: The history checked against Genesis and Exodus
deep.b:
The psalm follows the Torah closely but chooses and shapes what it tells.

The ancestors (105:8–15). The promise of the land to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob matches Genesis 15:18, Genesis 26:3 and Genesis 28:13. The kings rebuked are Pharaoh and Abimelech (Genesis 12:17; Genesis 20:3–7). The psalm calls the ancestors "prophets" as Genesis 20:7 calls Abraham.

Joseph (105:16–22). Genesis says Joseph was sold (Genesis 37:28) and put in the prison house (Genesis 39:20) but does not mention fetters or an iron collar (105:18), and does not say he taught Pharaoh's elders (105:22). The psalm's "he had sent someone on before them" (105:17) is Joseph's own reading in Genesis 45:5–8. "In charge of his household" (105:21) is from Genesis 41:40.

The plagues (105:26–36). Exodus tells ten blows in this order: blood, frogs, gnats, swarm, livestock, boils, hail, locusts, darkness, firstborn. The psalm has eight and puts darkness first: darkness, blood, frogs, swarm, gnats, hail, locusts, firstborn. It leaves out the livestock disease and the boils, and it reverses the swarm and the gnats. Psalm 78:44–51 has yet another selection and order. Neither psalm claims to give a list in sequence; both are poems.

The exodus and wilderness (105:37–41). The silver and gold (Exodus 12:35–36), the cloud and fire (Exodus 13:21), quail and manna (Exodus 16:13–15), and water from the rock (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11) all match. What the psalm leaves out is every complaint, rebellion and punishment: the grumbling at the sea, the golden calf and the forty years. Psalm 106 tells those.

settings.what: A hymn that retells Israel's history as God's faithfulness to his promise
settings.by: Unnamed singers; 1 Chronicles 16:7 has David give the first part to Asaph and his brothers
settings.to: The congregation, "you seed of Abraham" (105:6), and through them "the peoples" (105:1)
settings.when: Chronicles places 105:1–15 at the ark's arrival in Jerusalem, about 1000 BC; most scholars date the psalm after the exile, perhaps 500–400 BC
settings.why: To call Israel to remember that every turn of its history, even famine and slavery, served God's promise of the land, and that the gift came so that Israel would keep his laws
settings.readers: For returned exiles, few in number and living in a land ruled by others, the psalm's picture of the ancestors as "very few, foreigners living there" (105:12), protected by God, spoke directly to their own position.
views: Traditional readers follow Chronicles and hear the song of David's Levites.
Most critical scholars think the psalm is post-exilic and that Chronicles borrowed it (Allen; Japhet).

title: We Have Sinned with Our Ancestors
sum: The psalm opens with praise, "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; / his loyal love is forever" (106:1), and a single voice asks to be remembered when God restores his people (106:4–5). Then comes a confession: "We have sinned along with our ancestors" (106:6). What follows retells the history of Psalm 105 as a history of sin. Israel rebelled at the Sea of Reeds, yet God saved them for his name's sake; they believed and sang, then quickly forgot (106:7–13). They craved meat in the wilderness, envied Moses and Aaron, made a calf at Horeb and exchanged their glory for an ox, and only Moses, standing in the broken wall, kept God from destroying them (106:14–23). They rejected the land, joined the Baal of Peor and provoked God at Meribah; Phinehas stood up and the plague stopped, and Moses himself suffered for their sake (106:24–33).

In the land they did not destroy the Canaanites but learned their ways, served idols and sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons, until God handed them over to the nations (106:34–42). Again and again he rescued them, and still they rebelled; yet he heard their cry, remembered his covenant and made their captors pity them (106:43–46). The psalm ends with a prayer, "gather us from the nations" (106:47), and the blessing that closes Book IV of the Psalter (106:48). 106:1 and 106:47–48 are also in 1 Chronicles 16:34–36. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 105.
readings: Read as confession
The psalm is a long confession of national sin, like Nehemiah 9, Daniel 9 and Ezra 9, spoken by a generation that knows it shares its ancestors' guilt.
Read as hope

Every story of sin ends with God's mercy, and the psalm is framed by thanks for his loyal love (106:1) and a prayer to be gathered (106:47). Its point is that God's faithfulness outlasts Israel's failure.
Read with Psalm 105
The two psalms tell the same events, from the exodus to the land, from two sides: God's faithfulness and the people's unfaithfulness.

views.H: The Hebrew psalm has no title; the Greek has "Alleluia." Readers who take Chronicles' setting as history hear David's Levites at the ark singing 106:1 and 106:47–48 (1 Chronicles 16:34–36). Others note that 106:47 assumes a scattered people and read the whole psalm as a prayer of the exiles.
views.C: Critical scholars date the psalm to the exile or after, because of its prayer to be gathered from the nations (106:47), its closeness to Solomon's prayer for the exiles (1 Kings 8:46–50) and to Ezekiel 20, and its use of the finished Torah (including the Priestly material on Phinehas). The doxology (106:48) closes Book IV and was probably added or adapted when the books of the Psalter were arranged. Chronicles' use of it suggests that Book IV ended here by about 400–300 BC.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 105. 106:1 is one of the most used refrains of the temple and synagogue. 106:45 is one of the verses of remembrance (Zikhronot) in the Rosh Hashanah additional service, and the Hodu prayer of the morning service contains 106:1 and 106:47–48 through 1 Chronicles 16. Christians read the psalm in Lent, and the Benedictus (Luke 1:68) opens with the same formula of blessing, which is also found in 1 Kings 1:48 and Psalm 41:13.
views.J: The Talmud (Megillah 18a) draws from 106:2 the rule that one should not multiply praises of God beyond the fixed prayers. Rabbinic tradition counts the calf (106:19–20) as Israel's gravest sin and Phinehas (106:30–31) as the model of zeal rewarded with an eternal priesthood. Medieval commentators read 106:46–47 as a prayer still unanswered in the long exile.
views.X: Paul uses the same wilderness stories (craving, idolatry, Peor) as warnings in 1 Corinthians 10:1–11 and echoes 106:20 in Romans 1:23. Stephen's speech (Acts 7) tells Israel's history in the same accusing way. 106:31, Phinehas's deed "reckoned to him as righteousness," has been debated between Protestants and Catholics as a test case for justification (see below).

deep.h: The history checked against Exodus and Numbers
deep.b:
Psalm 106 tells eight episodes of rebellion. Each can be checked against the site's Plain of Exodus and Numbers:

Psalm 106TorahDifferences
Rebellion at the sea (106:7–12)Exodus 14:10–31; Exodus 15:1Exodus has fear and complaint; the psalm calls it rebellion.
Craving for meat (106:13–15)Numbers 11:4–34Close; the psalm calls the plague "a thinning sickness."
Dathan and Abiram (106:16–18)Numbers 16:1–35The psalm leaves out Korah (compare Deuteronomy 11:6).
The calf at Horeb (106:19–23)Exodus 32:1–14Close; Horeb is Deuteronomy's name.
Rejecting the land (106:24–27)Numbers 13–14The psalm adds an oath to scatter their children (compare Ezekiel 20:23).
Baal of Peor (106:28–31)Numbers 25:1–13"Sacrifices of the dead" for Numbers' "sacrifices for their gods"; Phinehas's spear is not mentioned.
Meribah (106:32–33)Numbers 20:2–13Numbers blames Moses' unbelief; the psalm stresses the people's provocation, like Deuteronomy 1:37.
In the land (106:34–46)Judges 1–2; 2 Kings 17; 2 Kings 21Centuries compressed into a pattern of sin and rescue, ending in exile.

The psalm's order is its own: the craving (Numbers 11) and the revolt of Dathan and Abiram (Numbers 16) come before the calf (Exodus 32), and Dathan and Abiram also come before the spies (Numbers 13–14). Many commentators see a thematic arrangement: sins against God's provision, then against his appointed leaders, then idolatry. The psalm agrees in substance with the Torah everywhere; its additions are interpretations, chiefly the reading of the exile back into the wilderness oath (106:27).

deep.b: Chronicles closes the song of 1 Chronicles 16 with 106:1 and 106:47–48. The differences are telling. Chronicles leaves out the opening "Praise the LORD!" (1 Chronicles 16:34). It introduces 106:47 with "And say" and changes "LORD our God" to "God who rescues us," and "gather us" to "Gather us and pull us out" (1 Chronicles 16:35). And it turns the command of 106:48, "let all the people say, 'Amen!' Praise the LORD!," into a narrative: "And the whole people said, 'Amen!' and gave praise to the LORD" (1 Chronicles 16:36). A prayer to be gathered from the nations is odd on David's lips; it fits the Chronicler's own audience after the exile. That Chronicles quotes the doxology of Book IV suggests that the Psalter's division into books was already known.

deep.title: Claude's theory: what Chronicles left out
deep.b: My own observation, not a view I have found in a commentary: the Chronicler's song takes from Psalm 105 exactly the verses that end before Egypt (105:1–15), and from Psalm 106 exactly the verses that frame its history of sin without telling any of it (106:1, 47–48). Joseph's chains, the plagues, the calf and the child sacrifices all fall in the gaps. The effect is a song of a covenant people protected while still "very few" (1 Chronicles 16:19), praising God among the nations (Psalm 96) and asking to be gathered: a picture of the Chronicler's own small community, with the long history of failure placed outside the festival. If this is right, the cut points are not accidents of quotation but a choice of what a worshiping community should sing at the ark.

settings.what: A communal confession of sin that retells Israel's history
settings.by: Unnamed singers; 1 Chronicles 16 places 106:1 and 106:47 in the mouths of David's Levites
settings.to: God, in the community's voice ("we," 106:6), with one voice praying alone (106:4–5)
settings.when: Most scholars date it to the exile or after, about 550–400 BC, since it prays to be gathered from the nations (106:47)
settings.why: To confess that the people's present ruin was the fruit of a long history of sin, and to appeal to the God whose loyal love had rescued them again and again
settings.readers: For Jews in exile or in the scattered communities after it, the psalm gave a way to own the disaster without despair: the same God who had relented in the wilderness and the land could make their captors pity them and gather them home.
views: Traditional readers follow Chronicles for the frame of the psalm.
Most critical scholars read it as a prayer of the exile, close to 1 Kings 8 and Ezekiel 20 (Allen; Kraus).

settings.what: The doxology that closes Book IV of the Psalter
settings.by: Probably the editors who arranged the Psalter into five books
settings.when: By the time of Chronicles (about 400–300 BC), which quotes it
settings.why: To close Psalms 90–106 with a blessing of God and the people's response, as Books I to III close (Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:18–19; Psalm 89:52)
settings.readers: Those who prayed the Psalter as five books, like the five books of Moses, heard each closing blessing as a pause; after the confession of Psalm 106 the people still say "Amen."
views: Some read the verse as the psalm's own ending, later used to mark the book's end.
Others think the editors added it to close Book IV (Wilson).

traditions.q: Phinehas's deed was "reckoned to him as righteousness" (106:31). Does this show that works justify?
views: Righteousness received in grace grows through good works done in faith; Scripture can call such deeds righteousness, as here, without denying that the first grace of justification is a free gift (Council of Trent, session 6, chapters 8 and 10).

No: people are justified freely for Christ's sake through faith, not by works (Augsburg Confession 4); Phinehas's zeal was the fruit of faith and is praised as such, but it is not the righteousness by which a sinner stands before God.

No: Calvin held that the deed was reckoned as righteousness because the person was already accepted by grace through faith, so that God approved the work for the sake of the one who did it; it does not earn acceptance (compare Westminster Confession 11 and 16).
The question is posed differently: salvation is union with God in faith that works through love, and the saints' deeds of zeal are signs of that life; faith and works are not set against each other.
